rows: Food businesses should prevent contamination from raw foods spreading to ready-to-eat foods.
Physical separation is an important control where practicable.
Complex equipment used for raw and ready-to-eat food requires suitable segregation or effective decontamination.
Hands, cloths, utensils and surfaces can transfer contamination.
Cleaning and disinfection procedures should be validated and consistently applied.
Staff movement and workflow should support separation.
Raw-food packaging and waste should be controlled.
Controls should be reviewed after layout, menu or process changes.
Colour-coded equipment or a cleaning record does not prove effective prevention of cross-contamination.
Conclusions require layout, workflow, equipment, cleaning chemistry, contact time, staff practice, verification and product evidence.
Raw drinking milk can contain harmful microorganisms because it has not been heat treated.
Production and sale are subject to specific hygiene and distribution controls.
Milk should come from eligible herds and controlled production premises.
Microbiological monitoring supports verification of hygiene.
Cold-chain control is important during storage and distribution.
Required health warnings should be provided to consumers.
Traceability should identify production and sale.
Adverse results or illness reports should trigger investigation and product action.
A farm registration or compliant sample does not prove that every raw-milk batch is safe.
Conclusions require herd health, milking hygiene, sample results, temperature, lot, label, distribution and incident evidence.
Shell eggs can present a Salmonella risk if production and handling controls fail.
Flock health and vaccination programmes can reduce risk.
Eggs should be kept clean, dry and protected from contamination.
Cracked or heavily soiled eggs require appropriate control.
Storage and handling should avoid damaging temperature fluctuations.
Traceability and producer marking support incident management.
Cooking advice should reflect consumer vulnerability and current official guidance.
Surveillance and testing inform risk management.
A lion mark, flock status or clean shell does not guarantee that an individual egg is free of pathogens.
Conclusions require production scheme, flock health, marking, shell condition, storage, cooking, consumer group and incident evidence.
Imported food must comply with applicable UK food law.
Import requirements depend on product type, origin and risk controls.
Some products require entry through designated border control arrangements.
Health certificates, laboratory results or prior notification may be required.
Importers should verify supplier and product compliance before shipment.
Traceability should link consignments to origin and distribution.
Official controls can include documentary, identity and physical checks.
Non-compliant consignments require controlled action and may be rejected, detained or destroyed.
A customs clearance or supplier certificate does not prove food-law compliance.
Conclusions require product, origin, establishment, certificate, notification, border checks, sampling, traceability and release evidence.
